To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the diffusion of innovation is driven by learning from peers and competition, and that the diffusion drivers are different for different types of innovation.
the diffusion of public management innovation is driven by a mix of learning, competition and public pressure.

the Berry and Berrys (1999) diffusion model has some explanatory power in explaining the diffusion of innovation among English local governments, but it does not have the same explanatory power for the diffusion of different types of innovations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how innovation spreads through the system.
the diffusion of public management innovations and the factors that influence the diffusion.
the diffusion of public innovation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diffusion theory has limited applicability for public management innovation.

the Berry and berry model of diffusion is best suited to explain the diffusion of total innovation, and that the model has limited applicability when explaining the diffusion of management innovations.
the Berry and Berrys framework is useful but not comprehensive enough to explain diffusion of all policy innovations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diffusion of innovation is a complex process that can be better explained by disaggregating the concept into types of innovation.
we have found the Berry and Berry framework is best used to analyze total innovation, but that the framework has limited application to types of innovation.
we found that diffusion is indeed driven by the same factors that are identified in diffusion theory.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the diffusion of innovation in the public sector may not be as similar to the private sector as is often assumed and that the drivers of innovation in the private sector may not be the same drivers of innovation in public sector.
the diffusion of public sector policy and management innovation types are more complex than is suggested by current diffusion literature.

the Berry and Berrys (1999) model has limited applicability in the diffusion of public innovation, and that future research should focus on the drivers of specific innovation types rather than on the diffusion of total innovation.
